children: High-yielding Latin American currencies will remain supported by carry trades even though their recent gains do not necessarily reflect improving economic fundamentals, according to Nur Cristiani, JPMorgan Private Bank's head of Latin America investment strategy.
are among the world's largest high-yielding currencies, while a move to support the U.S. Treasury bond market last month drove the dollar lower, making carry trades highly profitable.

"A year-to-date carry strategy in the Colombian peso, borrowing dollars and investing at Colombia’s overnight rate, would have generated about 27%, according to our calculations. That is more than double the return of the S&P 500
over the same period," Cristiani told the Reuters Global Markets Forum on Wednesday.
CHILE IS HER TOP PICK, BRAZIL HER MOST UNUSUAL ONE
's proximity to the U.S. and abundance of natural resources allow it to benefit from rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

Cristiani singled out Chile as offering the best combination of earnings growth, valuations and macro stability, citing a relatively stable economy, the completion of its easing cycle and strong terms of trade as copper prices have risen.
"We may start to see a more hawkish bias from the central bank, but that would be more toward the second half of the year and, in our view, would not derail the story," said Cristiani.
Brazil’s fiscal position is a key concern, particularly with the overnight rate close to 14%, making debt servicing costly for public finances, Cristiani said.
Despite the uncertainty, Brazil was her most "out of consensus" Latin American pick, citing current valuations.

Carry could remain well supported through the first half of 2027 regardless of the outcome of the October presidential election. But a stronger commitment to closing the fiscal gap could give the central bank more room to cut rates faster than expected, narrowing the interest-rate differential and bringing an earlier end to the trade, Cristiani said.
